Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Is the 2/ part of 2/14th Battalion (Aus.) A Second World War recognition of the First World War Battalion of the same area, place, etc.? So if called up again, would it possibly be 3/ 14th Battalion?
Answer: This is an interesting one. Normally, when we see a prefix such as 2/14th, we’d understand it to be the 2nd service battalion of the 14th Regiment, but this is not quite the case here. During WW1, the British Army underwent expansion and the number of battalions in a regiment increased, sometimes dramatically. For instance, the Northumberland Fusiliers (a regular regiment) eventually counted 52 war service battalions, and was surpassed only by the London Regiment (a territorial regiment created in 1908) which had 88 battalions. So, for instance, there was the 3/4th Northumberland Fusiliers, which was the 3rd service battalion raised from the 4th battalion of the Northumberland Fusiliers. Slightly more obviously, the US practice is to number battalions within regiments so the 16th Infantry (the equivalent of a Commonwealth brigade) had the 1/16th, 2/16th, and 3/16th battalions with the companies being lettered sequentially A-L (no J). During WW1, the Australian Army raised sixty infantry battalions, numbered sequentially. At four battalions per brigade, the 14th Battalion was therefore the 2nd battalion in the 4th Brigade of the AIF (Australian Imperial Force). The 14th served at Gallipoli and on the Western Front and was disbanded at the end of WW1 before being raised again in 1921 as a militia battalion. Under the Defence Act of 1903 men in militia battalions could not be forced to serve outside Australia or its territories unless they volunteered to do so. Men of the 14th Battalion at Ypres When the second AIF was raised at the beginning of WW2 it was an expeditionary force designed specifically for overseas service. The new battalions raised for this force were given a new numbering system designed to distinguish them from the militia force. Thus the 2/14th was specifically the 14th battalion on the 2nd AIF. Although tradition and logic would normally suggest that there should be a 1/14th, there was no such unit because of the structure of the numbering system did not follow the commonly used format. Both the 14th and the 2/14th were raised from the Melbourne area (Victoria) and so were closely related, with the 2/14th adopting the 14th’s yellow over blue colour patch. During WW2, the 14th battalion was eventually merged with the 32nd battalion to become the 14th/32nd battalion which served in New Guinea and New Britain, mostly on garrison duties, before being disbanded in 1945. The 2/14th served in Egypt, Palestine, and Syria before being redeployed to serve in New Guinea and Borneo. Men of the 2/14th at Kokoda Therefore, unusually in the normal run of things, it is correct to say that the 2/ does identify the battalion as part of the 2nd AIF whilst still maintaining the link to the original 14th battalion raised in the same area. I suppose that it is indeed possible that in a future conflict, Australia could raise a third AIF (or equivalent) and distinguish its battalions with the prefix 3/. There could yet be a 3/14th Australian infantry battalion.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: How did British pilots navigate during World War II without GPS or satellite technology? Did they use maps with grid coordinates or another method?
Answer: In WW2, pilots used maps, compasses, chronometers, sextants (celestial navigation), dead reckoning and just plain old looking out of the window. Larger planes had astrodomes from which the navigator could make sextant shots although, certainly later in the war, celestial navigation was very much a last resort. The elements of aircraft navigation are the air speed and heading of the aircraft, the wind velocity and direction at the current altitude, and the speed and track of the aircraft against the ground. Of these the accurate determination of wind drift is the most difficult problem, especially on long flights where there was no visible ground reference. Astrodome on a C-47 Taking a sextant sighting through an astrodome Where available radio navigation aids such as Gee, Oboe, and later H2S were also used. The Allies also used the Loran (US) and Decca (UK) long-range (which is what Loran stands for) radio navigational systems. Pilots used specialised slide rules, usually strapped to their leg, the most famous of which was the E6B, which was still standard issue when I was learning to fly in the 1990s. These slide rules allow the pilot to make calculations of many sorts, including the calculation of the effects of wind drift. I still have mine and it is entertaining to demonstrate the concept of a slide rule, particularly a circular one, to anyone under about forty. Below is a section of a navigational chart maintained by the navigator of a Lancaster bomber during a raid on the French port of Le Havre. The ‘x’ marks are Gee plots and the vectors drawn between them and the triangle plots are so that the navigator can calculate the impact of wind drift on the plane’s course. Gee was a hyperbolic VHF navigation aid using a master and two slave stations. The stations were synchronised so that they transmitted with a known time difference which created a series of hyperbolic lines. By measuring the time differences, the navigator could position the aircraft on the hyperbolic grid. The RAF also deployed medium frequency (300-400 kHz) radio beacons that the radio operator could take bearings on, allowing the navigator to take bearings on two beacons and, adjusting for the time between bearings, plot his position at the intersection. Earlier, there was the low frequency radio range, the predecessor of the modern VOR, where pilots could fly along a beam where a uniform tone could be heard. If the signal of a single letter (A or N) became audibly distinct, the aircraft would be turned as needed so that the modulation of the two letters would overlap again. This was similar to the Knickebein and X-Gerat systems used by the Germans to navigate during the Blitz. Individual airfields also used Pundit Beacons which used red lamps to flash a two letter code in Morse that uniquely identified the airfield. From 1942, there were also Eureka beacons that were used by ground troops to help aircraft, using Rebecca, locate their position for air drops. Pundit light in action This only skims the surface of the topic but, in conclusion, I’d like to mention my friend and neighbour, now sadly no longer with us, Arthur ‘Robert’ Smith, who, in 1943, at the age of around twenty and having never previously left the country, picked up an unarmed Beaufighter from Filton in Bristol and flew it, mostly alone to save weight, in stages to India. His journey took him from Filton to RAF Perranporth in Cornwall, across the Bay of Biscay (where he was chased down to sea-level by Luftwaffe Ju 88s), in a dog-leg out into the Atlantic, to RAF Luqa in Malta, to RAF Idris in Libya, to one of the RAF airfields near Cairo, to RAF Habbeniyah in Iraq, before the final leg to RAF Mauripur near Karachi. I’d dearly like to be able to pop across the road and ask him what navigational equipment he had, but sadly I can’t. Whatever it was, it was a damned brave thing to do at that age. Robert and friends on his 90th birthday

Question: Can you describe the experience of fighting in the hedgerows of Normandy? What materials were they made of and how large were they? Were there any instances of soldiers getting lost inside them?
Answer: Extremely dangerous for all concerned. The problem with bocage is that it is not simply a hedgerow, it is a hedgerow on top of a four to eight foot bank. The bocage is a network of small fields surrounded by these huge hedgerows and sunken lanes and an ideal place for infantry to dig in and create defensive positions. Typical bocage Lane through the bocage - not ideal tank country As well as being a severe problem for infantry, any tanks climbing the banks and bursting through the hedgerows were exposing their lightly armoured undersides and were easy meat for Panzerfausts. You can see the general effect illustrated here with Churchills of the Scots Guards. The eventual solution to fighting in the bocage was mixed infantry, engineer and tank teams supporting each other and working very methodically to break the German defences field by field. This process could include the use of various ad-hoc solutions such as the famous Culin hedgerow cutter and Rhino tanks to break through the banks without exposing the tank’s underside.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: What factors influenced the Allies' decision to land on Utah Beach instead of Omaha Beach during D-Day?
Answer: Well, clearly the Allies landed on Omaha and Utah beaches as well as Gold, Sword, and Juno beaches. Silly question, so on to a spot of D-Day trivia. In general, Normandy was chosen by planners because it lay within range of air cover from over 200 fighter fields in the United Kingdom and was less heavily defended than the more obvious Pas de Calais sector whilst still providing the shortest distance between Great Britain and the Continent. The Bay of the Seine had flat, sandy, load-bearing beaches, the necessary frontage, reasonable tides, at least some protection from the weather, and ready access to the hinterland. Sword and Utah, the beaches at each extremity of the landings, were added quite late in the planning process in December 1943. Adding these two beaches doubled the frontage of the invasion and necessitated a month-long delay so that the required landing craft and personnel could be assembled. Utah was added both because the whole scope of the invasion was increased and also because the Allies had their eyes on capturing the port of Cherbourg. US infantry landing on Utah Beach The American beaches were originally called X-Ray and Yoke from the phonetic alphabet. The names were changed by Bradley, the commander of the US First Army, in March 1944. Apocryphally, Bradley discovered that two soldiers doing some work for him were from Omaha, Nebraska, and Provo, Utah respectively. Why the beaches weren’t called Omaha and Provo, which would make more sense, I do not know. Apropos of nothing, I seem to remember having a very decent breakfast in JD’s restaurant in Provo in 1994. I remember it because it was either on, or very close to, the 50th anniversary of D-Day. The British beaches were originally named after species of fish, Goldfish, Jellyfish, Swordfish, and Bandfish. However, the Canadians objected to their beach being called Jelly and the name was changed to Juno instead. Band beach is the forgotten sixth beach and was the intended landing beach for 46 and 47 Royal Marine Commandoes for an assault on the German batteries at Houlgate (Battery de Tournebride) and Benerville (Mont Canisy). This operation was cancelled after the naval bombardment of the batteries as they were deemed to be no longer a threat to the landings at Sword.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Why did the United Kingdom declare war on Finland on December 6, 1941 (one day before the Pearl Harbor attack)?
Answer: Not just Finland. Great Britain declared war on Finland, Hungary, and Romania on the 5th December 1941. One can hardly blame the Finns as they had been attacked by the Soviets in the Winter War between November 1939 and March 1940, which led to the expulsion of the Soviet Union from the League of Nations. After a very poor initial showing in the face of Finnish determination, the Soviets prevailed by sheer force of numbers and the Finns were forced to sue for an armistice in which the Finns lost around 10% of their territory, including their second largest city, and 13% of their industry. During the uneasy peace that followed the armistice in March, the Finns sought alliances and eventually lighted on the Germans on the basis that the enemy of my enemy is my friend. German troops were stationed in Finland and when Operation Barbarossa commenced, on the 22nd of June 1941, the Soviets bombed Finland causing the Finns to declare war on the 25th of June starting what was known as the Continuation War. Finnish Stug IIIs The Finns signed the Anti-Comintern Pact in November 1941 but, unlike Hungary and Romania, never signed the Tripartite Pact. However, Finland joined German troops in attacks on the Soviet Union, including Operation Silver Fox against Murmansk, and this together with Finland’s refusal to discuss territorial concessions offered by Stalin, led the British, who were now allied to the Soviet Union, to declare war on Finland. The British declaration of war was pretty pro forma and the only action taken against the Finns was a token and largely pointless raid against the Finnish port of Petsamo, Operation EF, launched on the 30th of July 1941. Whilst the Finns were technically enemies, one can’t help thinking that most Britons probably sympathised with their predicament.
